prompt: The GDPR calls the rule that data is kept no longer than necessary storage ___.
Storage is cheap. Why does keeping old personal data still cost Ipê something?

choices.text: Leaks, requests and errors all grow with it
choices.why: Right. Bigger incidents, harder requests, staler data.

choices.text: Old rows slow every query down until the database stops answering
choices.why: No. Speed is not one of the three reasons.

choices.text: The ANPD charges a fee per year of data kept
choices.why: No. There is no such fee.

choices.text: Backups of old data are forbidden by the LGPD
choices.why: No. Backups are allowed, with a retention of their own.

prompt: Tax law requires five years and the purpose ended after one. How long does Ipê keep the invoice?

choices.text: One year; the purpose decides
choices.why: No. Another law requires keeping it longer.

choices.text: Forever, to be safe with the tax authority
choices.why: No. Past the legal period nothing justifies it.

choices.text: Five years, and no longer
choices.why: Right. The law is both the floor and the ceiling here.

choices.text: Until the customer asks for it to be deleted
choices.why: No. A deletion request does not override the tax obligation.

prompt: An order was placed in March 2020. Under the tax rule in `gov.retention`, from when may it be purged?
hint: The first day of the year after.

choices.text: March 2025
choices.why: No. That counts from the order date, nine months too early.

choices.text: 1 January 2025
choices.why: No. That counts from the start of the order's own year.

choices.text: Whenever the finance manager decides each year
choices.why: No. The rule is written down so nobody decides each year.

choices.text: 1 January 2026
choices.why: Right. Five years from 1 January 2021.

prompt: Why is `keep_for` an `interval` and not a text column?
hint: What does the purge do with it?

choices.text: Text columns cannot be classified
choices.why: No. Any column can be classified.

choices.text: The purge does arithmetic with it, and it cannot say "a while"
choices.why: Right. A type that refuses vagueness.

choices.text: Intervals take less space on disk than any text column of the same meaning
choices.why: No. Space is not the reason.

choices.text: The LGPD requires periods to be stored as intervals
choices.why: No. The law says nothing about types.

prompt: How many prescriptions were past retention on 1 July 2026, before the purge?
The tickets rule says no law asks for two years. Why write that in `basis`?

choices.text: So that whoever changes it later need not fear a law that does not exist
choices.why: Right. A business decision says it is one.

choices.text: Because the ANPD requires a basis for every period
choices.why: No. The ANPD does not review retention tables.

choices.text: To make the purge skip tickets
choices.why: No. The purge reads `keep_for`, not `basis`.

choices.text: Because tickets are sensitive data
choices.why: No. That is not what the column records.

prompt: Why is customer 4407's hold a row in `gov.legal_holds` rather than an e-mail to the database team?

choices.text: E-mails cannot be used as evidence
choices.why: No. That is not the reason.

choices.text: The court requires a database table
choices.why: No. A court requires preservation, not a format.

choices.text: The purge reads it every time it runs
choices.why: Right. An e-mail lasts until it is forgotten.

choices.text: So that 4407 can see the hold in their account
choices.why: No. The hold is internal.

prompt: The case ends and nobody fills in `released_on`. What has the hold become?

choices.text: Nothing; holds expire with the case automatically
choices.why: No. Nothing in the table knows the case ended.

choices.text: An erasure request
choices.why: No. It is the opposite: nothing is deleted.

choices.text: A breach of the tax rule, since the order is kept past five years
choices.why: No. Keeping longer than five years is a data protection problem.

choices.text: Indefinite retention by another name
choices.why: Right. A hold nobody releases keeps the data forever.

prompt: The LGPD allows keeping data for the regular exercise of ___ in judicial proceedings.
Put the purge's steps in the order the function does them.
items: Find the expired orders, skipping held customers
Delete items, payments, deliveries and returns

prompt: The first version of `gov.purge` used temporary tables. Why did the lab refuse it?

choices.text: Temporary tables cannot be created inside a function in PostgreSQL
choices.why: No. They can, given the privilege.

choices.text: Lesson 1 revoked TEMPORARY from PUBLIC
choices.why: Right. Arrays in variables do the same job.

choices.text: The purge ran out of memory while building the list of expired orders
choices.why: No. The error was about a privilege.

choices.text: OpenBao blocked the statement
choices.why: No. OpenBao does not see SQL.

prompt: After the purge, `overdue.sql` still finds 13 orders. Is the purge broken?

choices.text: No; they are customer 4407's, kept by the hold
choices.why: Right. The report counts the schedule; the purge obeys the hold too.

choices.text: Yes; every overdue row should be gone
choices.why: No. A hold keeps them on purpose.

choices.text: Yes; guest orders were skipped by mistake
choices.why: No. Guest orders were purged.

choices.text: No; the query counts rows in backups
choices.why: No. It counts the live tables.

prompt: How many orders did the purge delete?
hint: The last row of its result.

prompt: Which article lets Ipê keep `gov.sales_monthly` after the orders are gone?

choices.text: Article 7, I, because customers consented
choices.why: No. The totals need no consent; they name nobody.

choices.text: Article 48, on incidents
choices.why: No. That article is about incidents.

choices.text: Article 16, IV
choices.why: Right. The controller's exclusive use, anonymised.

choices.text: Article 18, VI, on deletion
choices.why: No. That is the right to delete.

prompt: Three cells of March 2020 count one order. What would Ipê do before publishing the table?

choices.text: Nothing; aggregates are never personal data
choices.why: No. A small cell plus outside knowledge can say something about a person.

choices.text: Encrypt the table with OpenBao
choices.why: No. Encryption does not change what a published number says.

choices.text: Ask each customer for consent
choices.why: No. There are no customers left in it to ask.

choices.text: Suppress or merge the small cells
choices.why: Right. Lesson 5's rule before data leaves the company.

prompt: What is the general pattern the purge follows for history the business wants?

choices.text: Copy, then archive
choices.why: No. An archive is still a copy of personal data.

choices.text: Aggregate, then delete
choices.why: Right. The statistics survive and the people leave them.

choices.text: Encrypt, then forget the key
choices.why: No. That is a different technique, crypto-shredding.

choices.text: Delete, then rebuild totals from backups
choices.why: No. That would restore the very data that was purged.

prompt: Why does `gov.audit_log` record both `session_user` and `current_user`?

choices.text: One is who connected, the other the authority they used
choices.why: Right. `current_user` alone would say ipe_owner for everybody.

choices.text: PostgreSQL requires both of them in any trigger that writes to a table
choices.why: No. Nothing requires either.

choices.text: They are the same, recorded twice for safety
choices.why: No. After SET ROLE they differ.

choices.text: One is for INSERT and the other for UPDATE
choices.why: No. Both are written on every change.

prompt: Why does the trail record which columns changed but not their values?

choices.text: Values do not fit in a text array
choices.why: No. They would fit.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids logging values
choices.why: No. It forbids nothing so specific.

choices.text: Values would make it a permanent copy with no erasure path
choices.why: Right. Every address and name it watched, forever.

choices.text: Old values are kept in the table's own history anyway, so a copy would be redundant
choices.why: No. An UPDATE replaces them in the table.

prompt: What protects the trail against the owner of `gov.audit_log`, who can disable its triggers?

choices.text: A third trigger that refuses DISABLE TRIGGER
choices.why: No. A trigger cannot stop its own table's owner from disabling it.

choices.text: Making the function SECURITY DEFINER
choices.why: No. That decides whose rights write the trail, not who may disable it.

choices.text: Nothing; the owner is always trusted
choices.why: No. A trail exists for the cases where trust is the question.

choices.text: Writing statements to the server log, shipped to another system
choices.why: Right. pgaudit, and a log the owner cannot reach.

prompt: Why did the platform need a second trigger for `TRUNCATE`?

choices.text: TRUNCATE is slower than DELETE on a table with triggers
choices.why: No. Speed is not the problem.

choices.text: PostgreSQL fires no row triggers on TRUNCATE
choices.why: Right. The strongest change went through the gap.

choices.text: The row trigger only covered UPDATE
choices.why: No. It covered UPDATE and DELETE.

choices.text: TRUNCATE bypasses every kind of trigger
choices.why: No. A statement-level trigger stops it.

prompt: Why does the trigger raise an exception instead of returning NULL?
hint: What does a BEFORE trigger returning NULL do?

choices.text: NULL discards the operation silently
choices.why: Right. A delete that did nothing and said nothing.

choices.text: Returning NULL is a syntax error
choices.why: No. It is allowed, and that is the danger.

choices.text: Exceptions are faster
choices.why: No. Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: NULL would delete the row anyway
choices.why: No. It would skip it, quietly.

prompt: In an append-only table, a correction is a new ___, never an edit to an old one.
Customer 112 asks for erasure. How does the append-only trail stay compatible?
hint: What does 112 mean without the customer row?

choices.text: The trail is exempt from the LGPD
choices.why: No. It is personal data like the rest.

choices.text: Its rows about 112 are deleted with a disabled trigger
choices.why: No. Nothing in the trail needs to change.

choices.text: It holds only the identifier, and erasing the customer row leaves it meaning nobody
choices.why: Right. The history survives and points at nobody.

choices.text: The trail is encrypted with the customer's key
choices.why: No. There is no per-customer key here.

prompt: Why do the platform's event and practice logs have no foreign key to the accounts table?
hint: ON DELETE SET NULL would do what?

choices.text: Foreign keys slow down inserts
choices.why: No. Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Accounts live in another database, which a foreign key cannot reach
choices.why: No. The reason is the erasure path.

choices.text: Events are written before accounts exist
choices.why: No. That is true of visitors, and not the reason.

choices.text: The key would try to update an append-only row on erasure
choices.why: Right. And the two obligations really would collide.

prompt: Last week's backup is restored. What must happen before anybody uses the restored database?

choices.text: Nothing; the backup was taken legally
choices.why: No. It holds rows the schedule already removed.

choices.text: Run the purge again
choices.why: Right. A restore re-applies the schedule.

choices.text: Notify the ANPD of the restore first
choices.why: No. A restore is not an incident.

choices.text: Every customer must consent again
choices.why: No. Consent is not the issue.

prompt: How does OpenBao's audit device keep a log that proves which token was used without holding it?

choices.text: It writes a keyed hash instead of the value
choices.why: Right. HMAC-SHA256: comparable, not reversible.

choices.text: It encrypts the token with the transit key before writing the line
choices.why: No. It keeps no recoverable copy at all.

choices.text: It deletes each line after a day
choices.why: No. Retention is separate from how values are written.

choices.text: It logs only the token's last four characters
choices.why: No. That is how card numbers are shown, not tokens logged.

prompt: Match each table of this lesson to what it records.

pairs.right: what may not be deleted yet

prompt: The purge removed 950 orders, and a 2020 sales extract sits on a shared drive. What does that say?

choices.text: Extracts are outside the LGPD because they are files
choices.why: No. A file of personal data is personal data.

choices.text: The purge should have deleted the drive's files too
choices.why: No. The purge cannot see what nobody declared.

choices.text: The database complies and the company does not
choices.why: Right. Retention reaches only the copies the lineage map lists.

choices.text: Nothing; the extract is a backup
choices.why: No. A backup has a retention window; this has none.
